gloss: be desolate, lie waste; be appalled; make desolate
summary: To be emptied and left without inhabitant, and to be stunned at the sight of it: the one root says both what happens to a land, a city or a sanctuary laid waste and what happens to those who look on it. Everyone who passes the ruin “will be appalled and hiss” (1Ki 9:8; Jer 19:8), the land lies desolate and keeps its sabbaths while Israel is in exile (Lev 26:32–35), and Yahweh promises that the desolate land will become like the garden of Eden (Ezk 36:34–35). The nouns שְׁמָמָה, שַׁמָּה and מְשַׁמָּה are the waste itself, or the object of horror a people becomes; Daniel's “abomination that makes desolate” (Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11) is the Roman desolation of Jerusalem and its temple that Jesus foretold (Mat 24:15; Luk 21:20).

words.gloss: be desolate; be appalled; make desolate; appal
words.summary: Eighty-eight times, in six stems. The two sides are one: a place is שֹׁמֵם when it is emptied of people, and a man is שֹׁמֵם when he is stunned and speechless at such a sight; the same form serves both (Ezk 26:16; 27:35; 28:19), and in Jer 2:12 the heavens are told to be appalled and “very desolate”. The participles of Daniel (שֹׁמֵם, מְשֹׁמֵם) are the one who makes desolate.

stems.gloss: be desolate, lie waste; be appalled; (participle) desolating, the desolator

senses.definition: Of land, roads, gates, a sanctuary or a mountain: to be emptied of those who live there or pass through; of a woman, to be left alone and childless; of a man, to be left desolate by grief.

evidence.note: “Mount Zion, which is desolate (שֶׁשָּׁמֵם); foxes walk on it”: emptied of people, given to wild animals.
“The roads of Zion mourn because none come to the appointed feast; all her gates are שׁוֹמֵמִין.”
“The mountains of Israel will be desolate (וְשָׁמְמוּ), with no one passing through.”
“The sons of the desolate one (שׁוֹמֵמָה) are more than the sons of the married (בְּעוּלָה)”: the forsaken wife, opposite the married; quoted at Gal 4:27.
Paul quotes Isa 54:1: “many are the children of the desolate (τῆς ἐρήμου)”, of the Jerusalem above.
“To make them inherit the desolate inheritances (נְחָלוֹת שֹׁמֵמוֹת).”
“Your waste places and your desolate places (וְשֹׁמְמֹתַיִךְ).”
“They will raise up the former desolations (שֹׁמְמוֹת) … the desolations of generation after generation.”
Edom rejoiced over Israel's inheritance “because it was desolate (שָׁמֵמָה)”.
“Because they made you desolate (שַׁמּוֹת) and crushed you from all around.”
“My sons are desolate (שׁוֹמֵמִים), because the enemy has prevailed.”
“Open your eyes and see our desolations (שֹׁמְמֹתֵינוּ) and the city called by your name.”

senses.definition: To be struck dumb with horror or astonishment at a ruin or a judgment, often with “hiss” or “shake the head” of the passer-by.

evidence.note: “I will make the land desolate, and your enemies who dwell in it will be appalled (וְשָׁמְמוּ) at it.”
Of the temple: “everyone passing by it will be appalled (יִשֹּׁם) and will hiss, and say, Why has Yahweh done thus to this land and to this house?”
“Everyone passing by it will be appalled and hiss over all its wounds.”
“Be appalled (שֹׁמּוּ), heavens, at this, and shudder”: parallel with שַׂעֲרוּ “shudder” and חָרְבוּ.
The princes of the sea “will clothe themselves with trembling … and tremble every moment, and be appalled (וְשָׁמְמוּ) at you”.
“All the inhabitants of the coastlands are appalled at you, and their kings shudder.”
“As many were appalled (שָׁמְמוּ) at you, so marred was his appearance beyond man”: of the servant of Yahweh.
“The upright are appalled at this.”
“Let them be appalled because of their shame, who say to me, Aha, aha!”

senses.gloss: (participle) desolating; the one who makes desolate
senses.definition: In Daniel the active participle stands with “transgression” and “abomination”: what lays the sanctuary waste, and the one who does it, on whom the decreed end is poured.

evidence.note: “The continual sacrifice and the transgression that makes desolate (הַפֶּשַׁע שֹׁמֵם), to give both the sanctuary and the host to be trampled.”
“Until the consummation, and that decreed, is poured out on the desolator (עַל־שֹׁמֵם).”
“From the time the continual sacrifice is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate (שִׁקּוּץ שֹׁמֵם) is set up, 1,290 days.”
“The people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary … to the end of the war desolations (שֹׁמֵמוֹת) are decreed.”
“When you see the abomination of desolation (τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως) spoken of by Daniel the prophet standing in the holy place.”

stems.gloss: be made desolate, be laid waste; be appalled

senses.definition: Of land, cities, highways, altars and sanctuaries: to be left empty and ruined, without passer-by or inhabitant.

evidence.note: “The beast of the field will bereave you … and your roads will be desolate (וְנָשַׁמּוּ).”
“The highways are desolate (נָשַׁמּוּ), the wayfarer ceases.”
“The streets of Jerusalem that are desolate (הַנְשַׁמּוֹת), without man and without inhabitant and without beast.”
“The land was desolate after them, with none passing through or returning.”
“Their streets are laid waste, with none passing by; their cities are destroyed, without a man.”
“Desolate it mourns to me; all the land is made desolate (נָשַׁמָּה), because no man lays it to heart.”
“Your altars will be desolate (וְנָשַׁמּוּ) and your incense altars broken.”
“The high places of Isaac will be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel laid waste.”
Ammon said Aha “over the land of Israel when it was made desolate”.
“The storehouses are desolate, the granaries broken down.”
“Those who ate delicacies are desolate in the streets.”
“Let their encampment be desolate (נְשַׁמָּה); let there be no dweller in their tents”: desolate is without dweller. Quoted at Act 1:20 of Judas.
“Let his habitation be desolate (ἔρημος), and let no one dwell in it”, from Psa 69:26.
“The desolate land (וְהָאָרֶץ הַנְּשַׁמָּה) will be tilled, instead of being a desolation in the sight of all who passed by.”
“This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden.”
“I, Yahweh, have rebuilt the ruined places and planted what was desolate.”
“They will make the desolate cities inhabited.”
“They will build the desolate cities and dwell in them.”

senses.definition: Of people: to be stunned with horror at a judgment.

evidence.note: “The heart of the king will perish … the priests will be appalled (וְנָשַׁמּוּ), and the prophets astounded (יִתְמָהוּ).”
“Those who come after will be appalled at his day, and those before seized with horror (שָׂעַר).”
“They will lack bread and water, and be appalled one with another, and waste away in their iniquity.”

stems.gloss: make desolate, lay waste; appal; be appalled

senses.definition: To empty and ruin a land, a sanctuary, a habitation, a vine, a household; above all of Yahweh's judgment, but also of enemies who lay Jacob's dwelling waste.

evidence.note: “I will make your cities a waste (חָרְבָּה) and make your sanctuaries desolate (וַהֲשִׁמּוֹתִי).”
“I myself will make the land desolate (וַהֲשִׁמֹּתִי).”
“They have devoured Jacob and laid waste (הֵשַׁמּוּ) his habitation.”
The same words: “they have devoured Jacob … and made his habitation desolate”.
“I will lay waste her vine and her fig tree.”
“I will make the land and its fullness desolate by the hand of strangers.”
“We laid waste as far as Nophah.”
“The hand of Yahweh was heavy on the Ashdodites, and he ravaged them (וַיְשִׁמֵּם).”
“Making you desolate because of your sins.”
“You have made desolate all my company.”
“I will make him (וַהֲשִׁמֹתִיהוּ) a sign and a proverb”: a desolation for others to stare at.

senses.definition: To fill others with horror, or to show oneself stunned and speechless.

evidence.note: “I will make many peoples appalled (וַהֲשִׁמּוֹתִי) at you, and their kings will shudder with horror over you.”
Ezekiel “sat there seven days, appalled (מַשְׁמִים) among them”.
“Look at me and be appalled (וְהָשַׁמּוּ), and lay your hand on your mouth”: stunned to silence.

senses.definition: The infinitive with suffix, “all the days of its lying desolate”: the land emptied of Israel in exile, keeping the sabbaths it was denied.

evidence.note: “The land will enjoy its sabbaths all the days of its lying desolate (הֳשַׁמָּה), while you are in your enemies' land.”
“All the days of its lying desolate it will rest, the rest it did not have in your sabbaths.”
“The land will be left by them and enjoy its sabbaths while it lies desolate (בָּהְשַׁמָּה) without them.”
“Until the land had enjoyed its sabbaths; all the days that it lay desolate it kept sabbath, to fulfil seventy years”: the word of Jeremiah.

senses.definition: Of Ezra on hearing of the people's unfaithfulness: stunned, desolate in grief, sitting motionless.

evidence.note: “I tore my garment and my robe, and plucked hair from my head and beard, and sat appalled (מְשׁוֹמֵם).”
“I sat appalled until the evening offering.”

senses.definition: The participle with שִׁקּוּץ “abomination”: what is set up in the sanctuary and lays it waste.

evidence.note: “They will profane the sanctuary, the fortress, and take away the continual sacrifice, and set up the abomination that makes desolate (הַשִּׁקּוּץ מְשׁוֹמֵם).”
“He will make sacrifice and offering cease, and on the wing of abominations one making desolate (מְשֹׁמֵם).”
“When you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not … then let those in Judea flee to the mountains.”
Luke's account of the same words: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation (ἡ ἐρήμωσις αὐτῆς) has come near.”

stems.gloss: be appalled, be desolate within; ruin oneself

senses.definition: To be stunned and dismayed in oneself: Yahweh at finding no one to intercede, Daniel at the vision, the psalmist's heart within him; in Ecc 7:16, to bring desolation on oneself.

evidence.note: “He saw that there was no man, and was appalled (וַיִּשְׁתּוֹמֵם) that there was no intercessor; so his own arm brought him salvation.”
“I looked, and there was no helper; I was appalled that there was none to uphold; so my own arm brought me salvation.”
“My spirit faints within me; my heart within me is appalled (יִשְׁתּוֹמֵם)”: parallel with “faints”.
“I was appalled at the vision, and none understood it.”
“Be not over-righteous … why should you destroy yourself (תִּשּׁוֹמֵם)?”

evidence.locator: Dan.8.13; 11.31; 12.11, שֹׁמֵם/מְשׁוֹמֵם → ἐρημώσεως; Dan.9.27 מְשֹׁמֵם → ἐρημώσεων; Lev.26.34, 35; 2Ch.36.21, הָשַׁמָּה → ἐρημώσεως

evidence.note: “The abomination of desolation (τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως) spoken of by Daniel the prophet”: the Greek of Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11.
“Know that its desolation (ἡ ἐρήμωσις αὐτῆς) has come near”: Jerusalem surrounded by armies.

evidence.locator: Isa.49.8; 54.1, שֹׁמֵמָה → ἐρήμου; Dan.9.17, הַשָּׁמֵם → ἔρημον

evidence.note: Isa 54:1 quoted: “many are the children of the desolate (τῆς ἐρήμου) more than of her who has the husband”.
Psa 69:26 (Hebrew נְשַׁמָּה, Septuagint ἠρημωμένη) quoted as “let his habitation be ἔρημος”.

parallels.note: Waste, ruin: cities made a waste and sanctuaries desolate.
To hiss: the passer-by is appalled and hisses at the ruin.
To be astounded: the priests appalled, the prophets astounded.

opposites.note: To dwell: desolate is without inhabitant; the desolate cities are inhabited again.
The married woman, against the desolate one.
The desolate land becomes like the garden of Eden.

phrases.gloss: everyone passing by will be appalled and hiss
all the days of its lying desolate

words.summary: Fifty-seven times, most often “become (or make) a desolation”, of the land of Israel, Jerusalem and the nations alike. BDB lists the same occurrences again under שִׁמָמָה (Ezk 35:7), counted here once.

senses.definition: A land or city emptied of people and left to wild beasts and weeds; what a land becomes under judgment.

evidence.note: “Lest the land become a desolation and the beasts of the field multiply against you”: emptied land goes back to the wild.
“Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without man, and the land is utterly desolate (שְׁמָמָה).”
“The cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.”
“Before it the land is like the garden of Eden, and behind it a desolate wilderness (מִדְבַּר שְׁמָמָה).”
“I made his mountains a desolation and his inheritance for the jackals of the wilderness.”
Joshua burned Ai “and made it a heap for ever, a desolation to this day”.
“Your land will be a desolation and your cities a waste.”
“Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation.”
“When seventy years are fulfilled … I will make the land of the Chaldeans everlasting desolations.”
“Instead of being a desolation in the sight of all who passed by.”
The northerner driven “into a land dry and desolate”.
“Your land will no more be called Desolation (שְׁמָמָה), but … Beulah, for Yahweh delights in you, and your land will be married.”

senses.definition: Desolation worn or drunk: the horror that comes on those under judgment.

evidence.note: “The king will mourn, and the prince will be clothed with desolation (שְׁמָמָה), and the hands of the people will tremble.”
“A cup of horror and desolation (שַׁמָּה וּשְׁמָמָה), the cup of your sister Samaria.”
“Behold, your house is left to you desolate (ἔρημος)”: Jesus over Jerusalem, before he foretells the temple's ruin (Mat 24:2).

words.gloss: desolation, waste; horror, object of horror
words.summary: About fifty times, mostly in Jeremiah: a land made a waste, and a people made “a horror and a hissing” to all who see them. The brief also counts here the name Shammah, which has its own entry, and the niphal verb נָשַׁמָּה by spelling.

senses.definition: A land, cities or houses laid waste and without inhabitant.

evidence.note: “Many houses will be a desolation, great and fair, without inhabitant.”
“To make your land a desolation; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant.”
“Her cities will become a desolation, with no dweller in them.”
“This whole land will become a ruin and a desolation, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years.”
“Desolation is left in the city, and the gate is battered into ruins.”
“It has laid my vine waste.”
“See the works of Yahweh, who has made desolations (שַׁמּוֹת) in the earth.”
“How they are brought to desolation in a moment!”
“Ephraim will become a desolation in the day of rebuke.”
“Your land became a desolation and a horror and a curse, without inhabitant, as at this day.”

senses.gloss: a horror, an object of appalment
senses.definition: A people or city so judged that all who see it are appalled: often with “hissing”, “curse”, “proverb” and “reproach”.

evidence.note: “You will become a horror (לְשַׁמָּה), a proverb and a byword among all the peoples where Yahweh drives you.”
“I will make this city a horror and a hissing; everyone passing by it will be appalled (יִשֹּׁם) and hiss.”
“I will make them a horror and a hissing and everlasting ruins.”
“A curse and a horror and a hissing and a reproach among all the nations.”
“That they would become a horror and a curse.”
“He has made them a terror, a horror and a hissing, as you see with your eyes.”
“How Babylon has become a horror among the nations!”
“How she has become a horror, a lair for beasts! Everyone passing by her hisses.”

senses.definition: The horror itself, that seizes the onlooker or the sufferer.

evidence.note: “For the breaking of the daughter of my people I am broken; I mourn; horror (שַׁמָּה) has seized me.”
“A horrible and appalling thing (שַׁמָּה וְשַׁעֲרוּרָה) has happened in the land.”
“The cup of horror and desolation.”

words.summary: The verbal adjective, hard to tell from the qal participle: the brief counts Daniel's שֹׁמֵם under both. Those are taken with the verb; the adjective proper is the desolate sanctuary, land, or person.

senses.definition: Left empty and ruined, of a sanctuary or a land; of a person, left alone and forsaken.

evidence.note: “Make your face shine on your sanctuary that is desolate (הַשָּׁמֵם).”
“Desolate (שְׁמֵמָה) it mourns to me.”
“Tamar remained desolate (וְשֹׁמֵמָה) in the house of Absalom her brother”: forsaken, unmarried and childless after Amnon's wrong.
“To the desolate wastes (הַשֹּׁמְמוֹת) and the forsaken cities.”
“He has made me desolate, faint all the day.”
“He has made me desolate.”

words.summary: Seven times, five of them in Ezekiel's pair “a desolation and a waste” (שְׁמָמָה וּמְשַׁמָּה).

senses.definition: Utter waste, paired with שְׁמָמָה to say the desolation is complete.

evidence.note: “I will make the land a desolation and a waste (שְׁמָמָה וּמְשַׁמָּה), and the mountains of Israel will be desolate, with none passing through.”
“A desolation and a waste, from the wilderness to Diblah.”
“The waters of Nimrim are desolations (מְשַׁמּוֹת), for the grass is withered, the greenery is gone.”

senses.definition: An object of horror to the nations.

evidence.note: “A reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror (וּמְשַׁמָּה) to the nations around you.”

senses.definition: The dismay of a besieged people who eat and drink by measure, parallel with דְּאָגָה “anxiety”.

evidence.note: “They will eat bread by weight and with anxiety, and drink water by measure and with horror (בְּשִׁמָּמוֹן).”
“They will eat their bread with anxiety and drink their water with horror, because her land will be desolate (תֵּשַׁם).”

senses.definition: Daniel stunned for a moment by the meaning of the king's dream, unable at once to speak it.

evidence.note: “Daniel … was appalled (אֶשְׁתּוֹמַם) for a moment, and his thoughts alarmed him”; the king answered, “let not the dream alarm you”.

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targums and Talmud: Ithpa. “be desolate” (Targ. Lam 4:5), “be confounded, mad” (Targ. 1Sa 21:14); Ithpol. “be perplexed”, citing Daniel 4:16; the adjective שַׁמָּם “confounded, demented”. Both sides of the Hebrew, waste and stunned bewilderment, in one Aramaic verb. Aramaic writes PS ṯ as ת, so its ש shows š.

evidence.locator: U01492, שְׁמַם (ch.), Ithpa. אִשְׁתְּמַם: 1) to be desolate, Targ. Lam 4:5; 2) to be confounded, mad, Targ. 1Sa 21:14; Ithpol. אִשְׁתּוֹמֵם, to be perplexed, Ḥull. 21a
U01493, שַׁמָּם, pl. שַׁמָּמִין, confounded, demented, Cant. R. to 4:7

cognates.note: Late (Seleucid) and medical; numbness or paralysis would answer to the stunned, motionless sense of the Hebrew (Ezr 9:3–4, sitting appalled). Akkadian š merges PS š and ṯ, so it shows nothing for the letter.

evidence.locator: armep x000095640; cmawro x000020510, šamāmu [injure] V: “be(come) numb; cause pain; paralyse”

cognates.gloss: put poison into, poison; سَمٌّ poison; سَمُومٌ hot desert wind
cognates.note: The Proto-Semitic list sets it beside שׁמם; the meaning is far from the Hebrew, unless through the scorching wind (سَمُوم) that leaves a land waste. Named on no word.

Only from the Proto-Semitic list; not yet checked in Dillmann. If it holds, it agrees with the Aramaic “confounded, demented” and the Akkadian “numb” on a stunned, senseless state. Ge'ez s merges PS š and ṯ.

doctrine.statement: Daniel is told that after the sixty-two weeks the anointed one will be cut off, and “the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary … desolations are decreed”; sacrifice and offering will cease, and “on the wing of abominations” comes one making desolate (Dan 9:26–27; also 11:31; 12:11). Jesus, sitting over against the temple and having said that not one stone would be left on another, names this very thing: “when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet standing in the holy place, then let those in Judea flee to the mountains” (Mat 24:2, 15–16), and he sets it within “this generation” (Mat 24:34). Luke gives the same words plainly: “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near … and Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles” (Luk 21:20, 24). So the anointed one cut off is Jesus, and the abomination that makes desolate is the Roman army that surrounded Jerusalem and destroyed the city and its temple in AD 70, ending the sacrifices as Daniel said; the house Jesus left “desolate” (Mat 23:38) was laid waste within that generation.

The law foretold that Yahweh would make the land desolate and scatter Israel among the nations, and that the land would keep its sabbaths “all the days of its lying desolate” (Lev 26:32–35, 43); Chronicles records it fulfilled in the seventy years (2Ch 36:21). But in the same chapter Yahweh says he will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, “and the land I will remember” (Lev 26:42). The prophets promise that the desolate land will be tilled and become “like the garden of Eden”, the desolate cities rebuilt and inhabited (Ezk 36:34–36; Amo 9:14–15; Isa 61:4), and that it will no more be called שְׁמָמָה “Desolation” but married to Yahweh (Isa 62:4). The desolation is a judgment for a time, not the end of the promise: the land itself, promised to Abraham, is to be restored and inhabited.

Twice Yahweh looks and is appalled (וַיִּשְׁתּוֹמֵם) that there is no man to intercede or uphold, “so his own arm brought him salvation” (Isa 59:16; 63:5). The arm of Yahweh is the servant at whom many were appalled (שָׁמְמוּ) because his appearance was so marred (Isa 52:13–14; 53:1), and John applies “to whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?” to Jesus (Joh 12:37–38). Salvation did not come from any man who could intercede of himself; God provided it, through the man he raised up as his own arm.

note: BDB keys: v.ea.ad (שִׁמָמָה) lists the same occurrences as v.ea.ac and is left out; the name Shammah (v.ea.ag, שַׁמָּא v.ea.ae) is in names/shammah.json. The brief's two verb tokens with no stem are שַׁמּוֹת: Psa 46:9 is the plural of the noun שַׁמָּה (cited there) and 1Ch 11:27 is the name Shammoth (Shammah the Harorite). Shammai (שַׁמַּי, v.ea.ai, 1Ch 2:28, 32, 44–45; 4:17) is left without a name entry: it may be of this root, or a short form of a שׁמע name (Shemaiah), and the text does not settle it; Shamhuth (1Ch 27:8) is probably the same man as Shammah the Harorite but spelled שַׁמְהוּת, not filed here. Daniel's שֹׁמֵם is counted by the brief under both the verb and the adjective; its senses are written under the verb's qal. Hiphil Jer 49:20 and 50:45 (יַשִּׁים) may be read “appal” rather than “make desolate”; filed under make desolate. Ecc 7:16 תִּשּׁוֹמֵם “ruin yourself” is placed with the hithpolel's appalled sense for want of a separate sense; it may deserve its own. Open: whether the core is “desolate” with “appalled” derived (the onlooker's reaction to a waste), or a stunned stillness behind both, as the Aramaic “confounded”, Akkadian “numb” and Ge'ez “silly” would suggest; Ge'ez samama not yet checked in Dillmann. The Aramaic אֶשְׁתּוֹמַם (Dan 4:16) is an ithpoel, the geminate root's form of the ithpaal; filed as ithpaal since the validator has no ithpoel. No Syriac שׁמם found in SEDRA (the Peshitta NT has none); Payne Smith not consulted. Dan 11:31 is stated in the doctrine with Dan 9:27 and 12:11 under Jesus' reference to “the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel”.
